summary.text: An ordered basis of an n-dimensional vector space lets you write any vector uniquely as a list of n numbers called coordinates.
Under a different basis the same vector usually gets different coordinates, and a change-of-basis matrix converts between them.
A new group of n vectors is a basis exactly when its change-of-basis matrix is invertible, which means it has a nonzero determinant.

facts.label: Coordinates
facts.value: A list of n scalars in an n-dimensional space

facts.label: Transition matrix
facts.value: Its columns are the new basis vectors written in the old basis

facts.label: Basis test
facts.value: The change-of-basis matrix must be invertible

facts.label: Standard basis
facts.value: Tuples with a 1 in one place and 0 everywhere else

facts.label: Physics use
facts.value: Often a rotation of an orthonormal basis, never a translation

items.prompt: Two surveyors describe the same location in a plane, each using their own pair of reference directions. What do you expect of their coordinate lists?

options.label: They are identical, since the location is identical
They are in general different
They are always negatives of each other
They are always in the same order but doubled

items.explain: The coordinate vector of a vector on one basis is, in general, different from its coordinate vector on another basis.

items.prompt: Once an ordered basis is fixed, how many coordinate lists can represent a single given vector?

options.label: Exactly one
Exactly two, one per direction
As many as there are scalars
None, unless the vector is zero

items.explain: An ordered basis allows representing any element of the space uniquely by a coordinate vector.

items.prompt: Someone writes n new vectors using an old basis and puts their coordinates into a matrix. Its determinant is zero. Do the new vectors form a basis?

options.label: Yes, any n vectors form a basis
Yes, but only for the standard basis
No, the matrix would need to be invertible
No, the determinant would need to be one

items.explain: The new vectors form a basis if and only if the matrix is invertible, equivalently if its determinant is nonzero.

items.prompt: In a change-of-basis matrix, what do the entries in column j describe?

options.label: The old basis vectors written in the new basis
The rows of the identity matrix
The j-th coordinate of every old vector
The j-th new basis vector written in the old basis

items.explain: The matrix columns are the coordinates of the new basis vectors on the old basis.

items.prompt: In the space of triples of numbers, which triple belongs to the standard basis?
items.explain: Each standard basis element has a 1 in one position and 0 in all the others.

items.prompt: A physicist turns the axes of her coordinate system to line up with a ramp, keeping the origin fixed. In mechanics, how is such a change of orthonormal basis understood?

options.label: As a rotation in physical space
As a stretching of physical space
As a shift of the origin
As a swap of two measurement units

items.explain: A change of basis in mechanics often transforms an orthonormal basis, understood as a rotation in physical space that excludes translations.
